items.stem: What is "automation bias"?
options: Over-trusting automated recommendations even when they are wrong
Bias in favour of robots in hiring
items.answer: Over-trusting automated recommendations even when they are wrong
items.markingKey: A. It weakens human oversight.

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "An AI system that is equally accurate for all groups is fair." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Equal overall accuracy can hide unequal types of error (false positives vs negatives) and unequal consequences; fairness also depends on how outputs are used.
items.markingKey: Equal overall accuracy can hide unequal types of error (false positives vs negatives) and unequal consequences; fairness also depends on how outputs are used. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between bias in data and bias in deployment.
items.answer: Bias in data comes from unrepresentative or historically unequal training data; bias in deployment comes from how a system is used – e.g. in which neighbourhoods, by whom, or with what level of human oversight.
items.markingKey: Bias in data comes from unrepresentative or historically unequal training data; bias in deployment comes from how a system is used – e.g. in which neighbourhoods, by whom, or with what level of human oversight. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"The algorithm was not designed to be racist. It was designed to predict costs, and in a system where less is spent on Black patients, cost became a biased measure of need."
— Summary of findings by Ziad Obermeyer and colleagues, Science, 2019

With reference to the source, explain how AI can be biased without discriminatory intent.
items.answer: The developers chose a target (cost) that seemed neutral but reflected unequal spending; the model learned that pattern, so the outcome was biased even without intent.
items.markingKey: The developers chose a target (cost) that seemed neutral but reflected unequal spending; the model learned that pattern, so the outcome was biased even without intent. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: An audit of a hiring model that shortlists applicants finds that 64 of 200 women and 78 of 200 men were shortlisted. Calculate the rate for each group and the difference in percentage points (a test of demographic parity).
items.answer: women 32%, men 39%; difference 7 percentage points

items.stem: With reference to the Obermeyer healthcare algorithm study (2019), explain how it illustrates proxy bias in AI.
items.answer: Researchers found a widely used US algorithm assigned Black patients the same risk score as white patients who were in fact healthier, because it predicted healthcare costs, which are lower for Black patients due to unequal access. A seemingly neutral target variable embedded structural inequality in a high-stakes health decision.
items.markingKey: Context (Researchers found a widely used US algorithm assigned Black patients the same risk score as white patients who were in fact healthier, because it predicted healthcare costs, which are lower for Black patients due to unequal access.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a seemingly neutral target variable embedded structural inequality in a high-stakes health decision. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to proxy bias in AI.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "AI should not be used in high-stakes decisions about people."
items.answer: AI can be used in high-stakes decisions only with strict safeguards – audits, transparency, meaningful human review and a right to contest; otherwise it should not be used.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: documented bias (Obermeyer, Williams); opacity and difficulty of appeal; automation bias weakens oversight. Arguments against: human decisions are also biased and inconsistent; well-audited AI can reduce some disparities; EU AI Act allows high-risk uses under strict conditions. Supported judgement: AI can be used in high-stakes decisions only with strict safeguards – audits, transparency, meaningful human review and a right to contest; otherwise it should not be used.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that AI bias is a technical problem that can be solved with better algorithms.
items.answer: Technical fixes help, but AI bias is fundamentally socio-technical and requires ethical, legal and institutional responses.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: fairness-aware algorithms and debiasing techniques exist; better data collection reduces errors. Arguments against: fairness definitions conflict and require value choices; structural inequality in society shapes data; deployment and power relations matter. Supported judgement: Technical fixes help, but AI bias is fundamentally socio-technical and requires ethical, legal and institutional responses. items.stem: Explain why different definitions of fairness can conflict.
items.answer: When groups have different base rates, a system cannot simultaneously give equal selection rates, equal error rates and equal calibration; choosing which to prioritise is an ethical and political judgement, not a technical one.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: When groups have different base rates, a system cannot simultaneously give equal selection rates, equal error rates and equal calibration; choosing which to prioritise is an ethical and political judgement, not a technical one. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: Equal overall accuracy can hide unequal types of error (false positives vs negatives) and unequal consequences; fairness also depends on how outputs are used.
items.markingKey: Equal overall accuracy can hide unequal types of error (false positives vs negatives) and unequal consequences; fairness also depends on how outputs are used. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: An audit of a hiring model that shortlists applicants finds that 82 of 300 women and 112 of 200 men were shortlisted. Calculate the rate for each group and the difference in percentage points (a test of demographic parity). Explain why equal rates (demographic parity) might not be the only fairness test, referring to "equal opportunity" (equal rates among qualified applicants).
items.answer: women 27.3%, men 56%; difference 28.7 percentage points; groups may differ in base rates, so parity may conflict with equal error rates; equal opportunity checks whether qualified applicants are treated equally – different fairness definitions can conflict (as in the COMPAS debate)
items.markingKey: 82/300 = 27.3% [A1]; 112/200 = 56% [A1]; |27.3 − 56| = 28.7 pp [A1]. Different fairness metrics (parity, equal opportunity, calibration) cannot all be satisfied when base rates differ; choice is a value judgement [R1 R1].

items.stem: Which 2023 strike won limits on the use of AI in writing film and TV scripts?
options: The Writers Guild of America strike
items.answer: The Writers Guild of America strike
items.markingKey: D. The agreement said AI cannot be credited as a writer.

items.stem: Explain why generative AI affects different workers from earlier automation.
items.answer: Earlier automation mainly replaced routine manual tasks (factories), while generative AI affects cognitive, creative and white-collar tasks such as writing, coding, translation and customer service.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Earlier automation mainly replaced routine manual tasks (factories), while generative AI affects cognitive, creative and white-collar tasks such as writing, coding, translation and customer service. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between augmentation and automation.
items.answer: Automation replaces humans in tasks; augmentation uses AI to support humans, making them more productive (e.g. AI-assisted coding).
items.markingKey: Automation replaces humans in tasks; augmentation uses AI to support humans, making them more productive (e.g. AI-assisted coding). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Only low-skilled jobs are threatened by AI." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Generative AI is highly exposed to tasks in professional work – writing, legal research, coding, design – so many high-skilled roles are affected.
items.markingKey: Generative AI is highly exposed to tasks in professional work – writing, legal research, coding, design – so many high-skilled roles are affected. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Klarna's AI customer-service assistant (2024) shows automation and job displacement.
items.answer: Swedish fintech Klarna said in 2024 its AI assistant was doing work equivalent to about 700 full-time agents; in 2025 it said it would hire more humans again to protect quality. AI replaced many customer-service tasks, but the later reversal showed limits of automation and the value of human service.
items.markingKey: Context (Swedish fintech Klarna said in 2024 its AI assistant was doing work equivalent to about 700 full-time agents; in 2025 it said it would hire more humans again to protect quality.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.markingKey: Occupation (translators, customer service, coders, illustrators); tasks automated vs augmented; evidence; interventions (reskilling programmes, collective agreements, Singapore SkillsFuture, universal basic income trials); judgement.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "reskilling"?
options: Training workers in new skills so they can move into different roles
Regulation that sets stricter rules for uses with greater potential harm, as in the EU AI Act
When generative AI produces works imitating a particular artist's recognisable style
Using machines or software to perform tasks previously done by humans
items.answer: Training workers in new skills so they can move into different roles
items.markingKey: A. "reskilling" is training workers in new skills so they can move into different roles.

items.answer: Through collective bargaining, writers set limits on how studios use AI, protecting credit and pay rather than accepting automation on employers' terms.

items.stem: "Governments should slow down the adoption of AI to protect jobs." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Rather than slowing adoption, governments should invest in reskilling, social safety nets and worker voice in how AI is introduced.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: gives time for reskilling and social protection; protects vulnerable communities. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A government body that tests and evaluates advanced AI models, such as the UK AI Safety Institute (2023)"?
items.answer: AI safety institute

items.stem: Explain why many experts argue voluntary AI ethics principles are not enough.
items.answer: Principles are vague, unenforceable and can be used for "ethics washing"; without legal duties, audits and penalties, companies under commercial pressure may ignore them.

items.stem: Zara writes: "The EU AI Act bans artificial intelligence." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It bans only a small set of "unacceptable risk" practices (e.g. social scoring, manipulative AI, most real-time remote biometric identification in public by police); most AI is minimal risk and largely unregulated.
items.markingKey: It bans only a small set of "unacceptable risk" practices (e.g. social scoring, manipulative AI, most real-time remote biometric identification in public by police); most AI is minimal risk and largely unregulated. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed so that the persons are informed that they are interacting with an AI system."
— EU AI Act, Article 50 (transparency obligations)

Explain why this requirement is important.
items.answer: It protects people from deception and allows them to judge information and relationships appropriately, which supports trust and autonomy.
items.markingKey: It protects people from deception and allows them to judge information and relationships appropriately, which supports trust and autonomy. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: With reference to the EU AI Act, explain how it illustrates risk-based AI governance.
items.answer: The AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024; bans applied from February 2025, duties for general-purpose AI models from August 2025 and most high-risk obligations from 2026–27. It shows a comprehensive legal approach that classifies AI by risk, with the potential to influence global standards (the Brussels effect).
items.markingKey: Context (The AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024; bans applied from February 2025, duties for general-purpose AI models from August 2025 and most high-risk obligations from 2026–27.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Compare two approaches to AI governance (e.g. EU, US, China, UNESCO) and evaluate their effectiveness in protecting citizens.
items.answer: Compare binding vs voluntary, risk-based vs sectoral, rights-based vs state-control priorities; examples; evaluate effectiveness and trade-offs with innovation; judgement.
items.markingKey: Compare binding vs voluntary, risk-based vs sectoral, rights-based vs state-control priorities; examples; evaluate effectiveness and trade-offs with innovation; judgement.

items.stem: Briefly explain why regulating general-purpose AI models is difficult.
items.answer: They can be used for countless downstream tasks by other developers, so risks depend on use; regulators must decide what duties fall on the model provider versus deployers, and capabilities change rapidly.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Generative AI threatens human creativity more than it enhances it."
items.answer: AI both threatens and enhances creativity; outcomes depend on rules on consent, compensation and attribution.

items.stem: Briefly explain why copyright law struggles with AI-generated works.
items.answer: Copyright traditionally protects original works by human authors; when AI generates most of the content, it is unclear who (if anyone) is the author – the user, the developer or no one – and whether training on copyrighted works was lawful.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Copyright traditionally protects original works by human authors; when AI generates most of the content, it is unclear who (if anyone) is the author – the user, the developer or no one – and whether training on copyrighted works was lawful. items.stem: Briefly describe the wrongful arrest of Robert Williams (2020) and explain what it reveals about AI bias and automation bias in policing.

items.stem: Explain the difference between inspiration and infringement.
items.answer: Inspiration is learning from or imitating general styles and ideas, which copyright does not protect; infringement is copying protected expression without permission or a legal exception.
items.markingKey: Inspiration is learning from or imitating general styles and ideas, which copyright does not protect; infringement is copying protected expression without permission or a legal exception. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "An AI system that is equally accurate for all groups is fair." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Equal overall accuracy can hide unequal types of error (false positives vs negatives) and unequal consequences; fairness also depends on how outputs are used.
items.markingKey: Equal overall accuracy can hide unequal types of error (false positives vs negatives) and unequal consequences; fairness also depends on how outputs are used. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between augmentation and automation.
items.answer: Automation replaces humans in tasks; augmentation uses AI to support humans, making them more productive (e.g. AI-assisted coding).
items.markingKey: Automation replaces humans in tasks; augmentation uses AI to support humans, making them more productive (e.g. AI-assisted coding). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the EU approach to AI governance and the US approach to AI governance.
items.answer: The EU uses a comprehensive, binding, risk-based law (the AI Act); the US has relied more on sector-specific rules, voluntary commitments, executive orders and state laws.
items.markingKey: The EU uses a comprehensive, binding, risk-based law (the AI Act); the US has relied more on sector-specific rules, voluntary commitments, executive orders and state laws. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between AI-generated work and AI-assisted work.
items.answer: AI-assisted work is created by a human who uses AI as a tool while making the key creative choices (likely protectable); AI-generated work is produced mainly by the AI with minimal human creative input (in the US, not copyrightable).
items.markingKey: AI-assisted work is created by a human who uses AI as a tool while making the key creative choices (likely protectable); AI-generated work is produced mainly by the AI with minimal human creative input (in the US, not copyrightable). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between equal opportunity and demographic parity.
items.answer: Demographic parity requires equal selection rates across groups; equal opportunity requires that equally qualified people in each group have equal chances of selection (equal true positive rates).
items.markingKey: Demographic parity requires equal selection rates across groups; equal opportunity requires that equally qualified people in each group have equal chances of selection (equal true positive rates). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"AI will affect almost 40 percent of jobs around the world, replacing some and complementing others."
— Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the IMF, January 2024

With reference to the source, explain the two different effects of AI on jobs.
items.answer: Replacement – some jobs or tasks are automated, causing displacement; complementing – AI augments workers, raising productivity and possibly wages.
items.markingKey: Replacement – some jobs or tasks are automated, causing displacement; complementing – AI augments workers, raising productivity and possibly wages. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Using China's generative AI rules (2023) as an example, explain AI governance and political values.
items.answer: China's Interim Measures for generative AI services (in force August 2023) require providers to register algorithms, label AI content and ensure outputs reflect "core socialist values". AI regulation can serve both safety and state control, showing that governance reflects political systems.
items.markingKey: Context (China's Interim Measures for generative AI services (in force August 2023) require providers to register algorithms, label AI content and ensure outputs reflect "core socialist values".) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: AI regulation can serve both safety and state control, showing that governance reflects political systems. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to AI governance and political values.

items.stem: Using New York Times v. OpenAI and Microsoft (filed 2023) as an example, explain AI and intellectual property.
items.answer: The Times alleged that millions of its articles were used without permission to train models that can reproduce its content and compete with it. The case tests whether training on copyrighted works is fair use, with major implications for creators and AI companies.
items.markingKey: Context (The Times alleged that millions of its articles were used without permission to train models that can reproduce its content and compete with it.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the case tests whether training on copyrighted works is fair use, with major implications for creators and AI companies. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to AI and intellectual property.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Obermeyer healthcare algorithm study (2019) and explain what it reveals about proxy bias in AI.
items.answer: Researchers found a widely used US algorithm assigned Black patients the same risk score as white patients who were in fact healthier, because it predicted healthcare costs, which are lower for Black patients due to unequal access. A seemingly neutral target variable embedded structural inequality in a high-stakes health decision.
items.markingKey: Context (Researchers found a widely used US algorithm assigned Black patients the same risk score as white patients who were in fact healthier, because it predicted healthcare costs, which are lower for Black patients due to unequal access.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a seemingly neutral target variable embedded structural inequality in a high-stakes health decision. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to proxy bias in AI.

items.stem: Outline one way in which a study of AI in customer support (Brynjolfsson et al., 2023) shows augmentation.
items.answer: Research on a generative-AI assistant for call-centre workers found productivity rose by about 14% on average, with the biggest gains for less experienced workers. AI acted as a tool that raised the productivity of novice workers, narrowing skill gaps rather than replacing workers.
items.markingKey: Context (Research on a generative-AI assistant for call-centre workers found productivity rose by about 14% on average, with the biggest gains for less experienced workers.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: AI acted as a tool that raised the productivity of novice workers, narrowing skill gaps rather than replacing workers. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to augmentation.

items.stem: Under the EU AI Act, fines for breaching obligations for high-risk systems can reach €15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. A company has a turnover of €900 million. Calculate the maximum fine.
items.answer: €27 million
items.markingKey: 3% × €900m = €27.0m [M1]; compare with €15m → €27 million [A1].

items.stem: Outline one way in which Théâtre D'opéra Spatial (2022) shows AI and the meaning of creativity.
items.answer: Jason Allen won the digital arts category at the Colorado State Fair with an image made using Midjourney; artists protested, and the Copyright Office later refused registration. The prize sparked debate about whether prompting AI is a creative act and what counts as art.
items.markingKey: Context (Jason Allen won the digital arts category at the Colorado State Fair with an image made using Midjourney; artists protested, and the Copyright Office later refused registration.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the prize sparked debate about whether prompting AI is a creative act and what counts as art. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to AI and the meaning of creativity.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "AI bias is a technical problem that can be solved with better algorithms."
items.answer: Technical fixes help, but AI bias is fundamentally socio-technical and requires ethical, legal and institutional responses.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: fairness-aware algorithms and debiasing techniques exist; better data collection reduces errors. Arguments against: fairness definitions conflict and require value choices; structural inequality in society shapes data; deployment and power relations matter. Supported judgement: Technical fixes help, but AI bias is fundamentally socio-technical and requires ethical, legal and institutional responses.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that AI will create more jobs than it destroys.
items.answer: AI may create as many jobs as it destroys in the long run, but transitions will be uneven and painful without reskilling and social protection.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: historically, technology created new occupations; new AI-related roles and productivity growth. Arguments against: generative AI affects a broad range of cognitive work quickly; new jobs may require skills displaced workers lack; gains may go to capital owners. Supported judgement: AI may create as many jobs as it destroys in the long run, but transitions will be uneven and painful without reskilling and social protection. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: "AI companies should be held legally responsible for harms caused by their systems." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Responsibility should be shared along the AI value chain, with clear duties for providers and deployers proportionate to their control.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they design and profit from systems; liability creates incentives for safety. Arguments against: harms often arise from users' misuse; complex supply chains complicate responsibility; excessive liability may deter open research. Supported judgement: Responsibility should be shared along the AI value chain, with clear duties for providers and deployers proportionate to their control. Markbands (8 marks): Markbands (five bands, scaled to the marks available): top – focused on the question; accurate use of Digital Society concepts, content and contexts; specific, well-explained real-world examples; balanced analysis of impacts and implications for different stakeholders; a clear, well-supported conclusion. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.

items.stem: Evaluate whether AI developers should pay creators whose works are used as training data.
items.answer: Arguments: fairness, consent, market harm, licensing deals (e.g. news publishers' agreements with OpenAI); counter: fair use, impracticality, benefits of open research; examples (NYT v OpenAI, Getty v Stability, EU opt-out); judgement.
